--- license: apache-2.0 license_link: https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0 pipeline_tag: image-text-to-text tags: - conversational - image-text-to-text - moe library_name: transformers --- # Inkling 2 Mini

Playground | Tinker Cookbook

## 1. General Information Inkling 2 Mini is a general-purpose multimodal model that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is intended for use in English and other languages, and across multiple coding languages. The model is designed to be used by developers building AI-powered applications, including agentic and tool-use systems, coding assistants, chatbots, and retrieval-augmented generation systems, and is suitable for general-purpose conversational use, instruction-following, and other natural language and visual tasks. It is released with open weights to support research, fine-tuning and integration into third-party products by downstream developers. **Languages:** English, general multilingual support **Model provider:** Thinking Machines Lab, Inc. **Date of release:** November 20, 2026 **License:** Apache 2.0 [Model Acceptable Use Policy](https://thinkingmachines.ai/model-acceptable-use-policy/) ## 2. Getting Started The weights are available for download through Hugging Face [here](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini). Developers can also access the model using the Tinker fine-tuning platform, which provides API access. * For accessing our model via Tinker, you can get started by referring to the Tinker Cookbook [here](https://github.com/thinking-machines-lab/tinker-cookbook), and installing the tml-renderers package [here](https://pypi.org/project/tml-renderers/). * Tinker playground also provides inference-only access to the model [here](https://tinker.thinkingmachines.ai/playground). ### Required hardware The model is distributed as a single checkpoint of about 20GB, in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 precisions. Given its small size, it is possible to run this checkpoint on local AI compute for inference. We support: * 1x NVIDIA DGX Spark * Apple silicon devices with 32GB or more memory (MacBooks, Mac minis and Studios) * Other GPUs and platforms are possible, with 32GB or more of VRAM recommended ### Required software Inkling 2 Mini supports inference using the following frameworks, along with their dependency libraries: * [Hugging Face](https://hf.co/blog/inkling2mini) * [SGLang](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/ThinkingMachines/Inkling-2-Mini) * [vLLM](https://recipes.vllm.ai/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini) * [TokenSpeed](https://lightseek.org/tokenspeed/recipes/models#inkling-2-mini) * NVIDIA Dynamo * [Unsloth](https://unsloth.ai/docs/inkling-2-mini), including quantized GGUF versions * llama.cpp, for quantized GGUF versions * [Llama App](https://llama.app/) On Apple Silicon * [Ollama](https://ollama.com/library/inkling-2-mini) and Exo Labs Inkling 2 Mini can also be post-trained with: * [Miles](https://miles.radixark.com/docs/models/thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini) * [SkyRL](https://docs.skyrl.ai/docs/models/inkling2) ## 3. Model Properties ### Model type Multimodal autoregressive looped transformer ### Architecture type A 24-layer decoder-only transformer with sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layers. The middle 12 layers run three times with shared weights, giving 48 layer applications per token from 24 layers of weights. In each layer, each token is routed to 8 of 128 experts. Attention is a hybrid of local and global layers. The model is natively multimodal – images are encoded via a vision transformer – with image and text inputs projected into a shared hidden space and processed jointly by the decoder. ### Parameters 26.4B, 3.4B active Note: each extra pass through the looped layers adds about 1.0B effective active parameters. Since the model runs with three passes, there are 5.4B effective active parameters per token. ### Numerics support NVFP4 and MXFP8 ### Input modalities * Text: UTF-8 encoded text * Image: Any pixel-based image input. For optimal performance, each image dimension should be between 40px to 4096px. Inkling 2 Mini supports a context window of up to 1M tokens. ### Output modalities Text ## 4. Training Training data includes a broad variety of content types, including text, images, video. Training data for the model was drawn from publicly available sources, acquired from third-parties, generated internally, or synthetically generated or augmented. Publicly available data includes content from the public internet and publicly accessible repositories. Data curation includes cleaning, processing, and modifying datasets. These processing steps, which vary by data type, may include deduplication and filtering to remove junk or other low-quality data, or to advance safety or other objectives. ## 5. Evaluations
Inkling 2 MiniGemma 4 31BMuse GlimmerQwen3.8-27BNemotron 3.5 Super VL

models.readme_content:
--- license: apache-2.0 library_name: inworld-voice-isolation pipeline_tag: audio-to-audio tags: [audio, speech, speech-enhancement, speech-denoising, noise-suppression, voice-isolation, 48khz, full-band, streaming, realtime] ---

Voice Isolator

Open-license (Apache-2.0) 48 kHz voice isolation for noisy speech recordings and live audio.

--- ## TL;DR Inworld Voice Isolator v1 ships as two models that share one architecture: | | `voice-isolator-v1` | `voice-isolator-v1-realtime` | |---|---|---| | made for | recorded audio and anything not latency-sensitive, at the best quality | live audio, as a stream in your pipeline or production | | how it runs | offline: every frame sees its whole 8 s chunk | a causal stream with 20 ms of look-ahead | | parameters | 64M | 58M | **Use them for** cleaning recordings before playback or publication, curating speech datasets and voice pipelines where the speaker's identity must survive. With the realtime model, use them for live calls and streams. Subtract the isolated voice from the input to extract background noise or a backing-track residual for vocals/music separation. **They are not** a speaker selector or a restoration model. Restoration is planned for version 2 (see [Plans](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator#plans)). ## Quick start Using a coding agent? Point it at the [setup section of AGENTS.md](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator/blob/main/AGENTS.md#setting-up-the-voice-isolator-for-a-user): it installs the package, checks the machine with `voice-isolate-doctor` and cleans a first file. ```bash pip install inworld-voice-isolation # or from a clone: git clone https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator && cd voice-isolator && pip install -e . # a noisy example; a clone also has it at demo/examples/sample_14.wav curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator/main/demo/examples/sample_14.wav # offline isolation (downloads the offline model on first use): # the voice goes to sample_14_clean.wav and the removed background # to sample_14_clean_background.wav, beside it voice-isolate sample_14.wav sample_14_clean.wav ``` Both are float32 WAVs at 48 kHz, with their original levels preserved; together they reconstruct the aligned mono input. Use `--output-sr 0` to keep the input rate, `--background noise.wav` to choose the background path for one file, or `--no-background` to save only the voice. ```python from inworld import voice_isolation # isolate a recording offline offline = voice_isolation.VoiceIsolator("inworld/voice-isolator") wav, sample_rate = voice_isolation.load_audio("sample_14.wav") voice = offline.isolate(wav, sample_rate) voice_isolation.save_audio("sample_14_clean.wav", voice, sample_rate, subtype="FLOAT") voice_isolation.save_audio("sample_14_clean_background.wav", wav - voice, sample_rate, subtype="FLOAT") # what was removed ``` ### Streaming The realtime model isolates the voice as the audio arrives, with 20 ms of look-ahead: ```python import torch from inworld import voice_isolation live = voice_isolation.VoiceIsolator("inworld/voice-isolator", mode="streaming", lookahead_frames=2) session = live.stream() # takes 48 kHz mono, in pieces of any size wav, sample_rate = voice_isolation.load_audio("sample_14.wav") # 48 kHz mono, standing in for a live source voice = [] for start in range(0, len(wav), 960): # 20 ms at a time, as a microphone delivers it voice.append(session.push(wav[start:start + 960])) # the samples that are final: play or send them voice.append(session.flush()) # the rest, once the source ends voice_isolation.save_audio("sample_14_streamed.wav", torch.cat(voice), sample_rate) ``` The streaming CLI writes only the isolated voice, after the whole file has gone through: ```bash voice-isolate sample_14.wav sample_14_streamed.wav --mode streaming --lookahead 2 ``` The weights download on first use, and their checksums are verified. The mode picks the checkpoint: `voice-isolator-v1` offline, `voice-isolator-v1-realtime` for streaming. CUDA is used when available, Apple's Metal backend (`mps`) on an Apple-silicon Mac with PyTorch 2.6 or later, and the CPU otherwise; `--device` picks one. The code, the [interactive demo](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator/blob/main/demo/README.md) and the [benchmark](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator/blob/main/bench/README.md) are on GitHub: [inworld-ai/voice-isolator](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator). The demo loads both models at startup: **Offline** processes files and samples into voice and background audio; **Online** streams the microphone for up to 60 seconds with updating waveforms and spectrograms, pausing capture before playback. ## Hardware Tested on NVIDIA Ampere, Hopper and Blackwell GPUs (A100, H100, B200 and B300) and on CPU. Smaller GPUs are not tested yet (see [Plans](https://github.com/inworld-ai/voice-isolator#plans)). ## The VIBE benchmark

--- license: apache-2.0 base_model: thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini pipeline_tag: image-text-to-text tags: - gguf - llama.cpp - inkling2 - uncensored - lora --- # Inkling-2-Mini Uncensored GGUF
  • Learn how to run Inkling 2 Mini Uncensored locally - read our guide.
  • Built by the team behind Atomic Chat, the app that runs open-weight models locally and offline.
An uncensored build of [thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini) by AtomicChat (26.4B MoE, 3.4B active, looped core; text and image input; Apache-2.0, LICENSE in this repo). It comes as a LoRA adapter for any GGUF of [AtomicChat/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/AtomicChat/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF) and as three ready-made GGUF files with the edit baked in. Every gate we hold it to is measured below, and the two it misses are shown. ## Files | file | GB on disk | KLD to the original BF16 | top-1 | | |---|---:|---:|---:|---| | `Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-AD-Q4_K.gguf` | 16.53 | 0.0115 | 95.6% | AD-Q4_K in the base repo: 0.0080 / 96.3% | | `Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-AD-IQ3_S.gguf` | 13.34 | 0.0235 | 93.8% | AD-IQ3_S in the base repo: 0.0205 / 94.2% | | `Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-AD-IQ2_M.gguf` | 8.67 | 0.132 | 85.7% | AD-IQ2_M in the base repo: 0.130 / 85.7% | | `Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-LoRA.gguf` | 0.04 | | | the adapter, for any GGUF of the base repo, BF16 to 1-bit | | `mmproj-Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-F16.gguf` / `-BF16.gguf` | 0.64 | | | vision projector (the original's, unchanged) | KLD and top-1 are against the original BF16 on our neutral corpus (87 chunks of 4096 tokens), the same stand as the base repo. ## Run it The current GGUF files in this repository use the merged Inkling 2 loop architecture introduced in [llama.cpp PR #32694](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/32694). **Requirements:** llama.cpp b12600 or newer, with Inkling 2 loop architecture support. The old implementation from [PR #32695](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/32695) is no longer required for the updated GGUF files. ### Run a baked GGUF ```bash ./build/bin/llama-server \ -m Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-AD-Q4_K.gguf \ --mmproj mmproj-Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-F16.gguf \ --jinja -c 32768 -ngl 99 ``` ### Run a baked GGUF with DSpark [Download the optional Q8_0 drafter](https://huggingface.co/AtomicChat/Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-GGUF/resolve/main/dspark-Inkling-2-Mini-Q8_0.gguf) (481 MiB). > **Running this drafter currently requires a llama.cpp build from [PR #32218](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/32218).** We tested commit [`e4b1cb5`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/e4b1cb5318f1ac55d148be228c6347c6a94cc4c6). Follow the [CUDA build instructions](https://huggingface.co/AtomicChat/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF#run-with-dspark-on-cuda) to build that commit, then run these commands from the llama.cpp checkout. ```bash hf download AtomicChat/Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-GGUF \ Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-AD-Q4_K.gguf dspark-Inkling-2-Mini-Q8_0.gguf \ --local-dir inkling-uncensored ./build/bin/llama-server \ -m inkling-uncensored/Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-AD-Q4_K.gguf \ -md inkling-uncensored/dspark-Inkling-2-Mini-Q8_0.gguf \ --spec-type draft-dspark --spec-draft-n-max 3 \ -ngl 99 -ngld 99 -fa on -c 4096 -np 1 --jinja ``` #### A100 results We ran three greedy text prompts (code, explanation, and JSON) on one A100 SXM4 40 GB at a 4,096-token context, one request at a time, with 192 generated tokens per prompt. Decode throughput is total generated tokens divided by total decode time. Peak VRAM was sampled every 200 ms. | Baked `AD-Q4_K` | Decode tok/s | Peak VRAM | Draft tokens accepted | |---|---:|---:|---:| | DSpark off | 46.5 | 16.42 GiB | — | | DSpark Q8_0 | **59.9 (+29.0%)** | 17.79 GiB | 42.7% (321/751) | The greedy token sequences differed between the two modes on all three prompts. We also ran one 64-token completion with each smaller baked quant. `AD-IQ3_S` accepted 35 of 82 draft tokens and `AD-IQ2_M` accepted 41 of 65. ### Use the LoRA adapter Use the updated LoRA adapter with a compatible base GGUF converted to the merged PR #32694 layout. ```bash ./build/bin/llama-server \ -m Inkling-2-Mini-AD-Q4_K.gguf \ --lora Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-LoRA.gguf \ --mmproj mmproj-Inkling-2-Mini-F16.gguf \ --jinja -c 32768 -ngl 99 ``` Do not mix GGUF files from the old PR #32695 layout with the merged PR #32694 implementation. ## What the edit is A rank-1 LoRA on the 49 places that write into the residual stream: the attention output and the routed experts of all 24 layers, plus the token embedding. **Sulphur 3**

An uncensored video generation model based on MiniMax H3.

Follow us on **[X](https://x.com/FusionCow11)**

Join our **[Discord](https://discord.gg/C3d56f39Ah)**

---

**Get Started:**

Download `s3.safetensors` and run it like any regular MiniMax H3 model. That's all you need, everything else in this repo is optional.

We also include lower vram options in `quantized/`

**Corrector (optional):**

This repo includes a corrector file which is OPTIONAL to use. You can literally just run s3 as a regular MiniMax H3 model, but if you do decide to use the corrector, `S3_ComfyUI.zip` has the necessary nodes and workflow. The corrector goes in `ComfyUI/models/h3_correctors/`. It also works with other H3 models.

**Alternative Models:**

Just to note, others have made checkpoints that include sulphur, I do go recommend you check them out. Prominently, I recommend [Tenstrip's Merges](https://huggingface.co/TenStrip).

---

**Files**

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `s3.safetensors` | Please use this one |
| `s3_raw.safetensors` | Sulphur 3 without the RL lora |
| `s3_ref2va.safetensors` | Ref2VA variant, not trained |
| `s3_raw_lora.safetensors` | `s3_raw` as a LoRA. |
| `s3_corrector.safetensors` | Optional corrector, see above. |
| `S3_ComfyUI.zip` | ComfyUI nodes and workflow for the corrector. |

**Experimental** (`experimental/`)

There's also a bunch of experimental files, you're welcome to try them out, though I'd recommend ignoring them.

---

**License**

Sulphur 3 is a derivative of MiniMax H3 and is released under the MiniMax H3 Community License. See `LICENSE`.

models.name: Ternary-Bonsai-2.5-27B-GGUF
models.readme_content:
--- license: apache-2.0 library_name: llama.cpp pipeline_tag: text-generation tags: - ternary - 2-bit - gguf - llama-cpp - cuda - metal - on-device - hybrid-attention - agentic - tool-calling - speculative-decoding - mtp - prismml - bonsai base_model: - Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B ---

Prism ML Website  |  Whitepaper  |  Demo & Examples  |  Discord

# Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B — GGUF A 27B ternary model built for agents, for llama.cpp (CUDA, Metal, CPU) > **\~9×** smaller than FP16 | **FP16-level** agentic tool calling | **90%** of FP16 agentic coding | the **strongest agentic model under 10 GB** Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B is the agentic release of the Ternary Bonsai 27B line. It keeps the Qwen3.8-27B hybrid-attention architecture and the ternary weight format of Bonsai 2, so it is still **1.76 bits per weight** and **5.93 GB**, against 53.8 GB for the FP16 model. This release targets long-horizon, tool-driven work. ## Highlights - **FP16-level agentic tool calling at one ninth of the size**: across five tool-calling benchmarks (τ²-Bench, τ³-Bench, BFCL v3, BFCL v4, and AppWorld), Bonsai 2.5 averages **77.2**, against **77.7** for FP16 — essentially indistinguishable from full precision - **90% of FP16 on agentic coding, up from 63% for Bonsai 2**: on Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Verified, and DeepSWE, DeepSWE rises from 0 to **27.0**, SWE-bench Verified from 60.8 to **75.6**, and Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 52.8 to **60.1** - **The strongest agentic model under 10 GB**: the smallest of the low-bit GGUF builds of Qwen3.8-27B we compare against, and it leads every build under 10 GB on both tool calling and agentic coding. Against GSQ-RCO IQ3_XXS, which is 1.7× larger, it is ahead on tool calling (77.2 vs. 75.3) and close on coding (54.2 vs. 55.5) - **General capability stays close to FP16**: averaged over five categories (16 benchmarks), Bonsai 2.5 scores **82.1** against 84.3 for FP16 - **Multi-token prediction (MTP) variants**: the MTP variants include a draft head that speeds up decode by **1.5–1.8×** on NVIDIA GPUs - **2.3–3.0× faster decode than on Bonsai 2's release day** on six of the seven NVIDIA GPUs measured, with MTP and the kernels now in testing — reaching about **300 tokens/s** on H200 and B200 - **Runs on stock llama.cpp**: the `Q2_0` files run on upstream llama.cpp; `PTQ1_0` is under upstream review ## Resources - **[Whitepaper](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo/blob/main/bonsai-2-5-27b-whitepaper.pdf)** — benchmarks, evaluation setup, and inference-speed measurements for this release - **[Bonsai 2 27B whitepaper](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo/blob/main/bonsai-2-27b-whitepaper.pdf)** — the ternary format, storage accounting, and rotated weight basis, all unchanged in Bonsai 2.5 - **[Demo & examples](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo)** — **the source of truth for running these models**: tested setup for every backend, pinned binaries, serving, MTP speculative decoding, benchmarking and integration, kept current as the runtimes move - **Low-bit kernels**: [llama.cpp fork](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp) (CUDA + Metal) · [MLX fork](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/mlx) (Apple Silicon) · [mlx-swift fork](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/mlx-swift) (iOS/macOS) - **[Discord](https://discord.gg/prismml)** — join the community for support, discussion, and updates ## Model Overview Changes from Bonsai 2 are marked with †. | Item | Specification | | :--------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Base model | Qwen3.8-27B, a 27B hybrid-attention causal language model | | Parameters | 24.35B language (64 blocks) + 0.47B vision tower (27 blocks) + 2.54B embedding/lm-head = 27.36B total | | Architecture | Hybrid attention (\~75% linear / \~25% full attention), SwiGLU MLP, RoPE, RMSNorm | | Context length | 262K tokens | | Weight format | Ternary g128 (FP16 group-wise scaling) in a blockwise Hadamard basis; 1.76 bits per weight, 5.93 GB (PTQ1_0) | | Focus † | Agentic and tool-use tasks | | Reasoning efforts | `xhigh` (default, most accurate) or `medium` | | Backends | llama.cpp (CUDA, Metal, CPU, SYCL) and MLX (Python, Swift); GGUF packs PTQ1_0 and PQ2_0, plus Q2_0 for stock llama.cpp | | Speculative decoding † | The MTP variants include a multi-token prediction (MTP) draft head | | License | Apache 2.0 | ## Weight Representation: Ternary g128 The released weights are exactly ternary and use the Bonsai 2 format, unchanged. Each weight takes a value from {−1, 0, +1}, with one shared FP16 scale factor for every group of 128 weights; a ternary value carries log₂3 ≈ 1.585 bits of information. The weights are stored in a **rotated basis**: each matrix is transformed blockwise by an orthogonal Hadamard rotation before the ternary assignment, and the runtime applies the matching transform to activations. The rotation is folded into the stored weights offline, so it costs no extra bits and no extra weight traffic.

--- license: other license_name: apple-amlr license_link: https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-depth-pro-2/blob/main/LICENSE_MODEL pipeline_tag: depth-estimation library_name: depth-pro-2 tags: - depth-estimation - metric-depth - monocular-depth - video-depth ---

Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth

Depth Pro 2 estimates metric depth for every pixel from an ordinary camera: a single photo, a whole video, or a live feed, at the input's full resolution. Its depth is sharp at object edges and steady from frame to frame. ## Models Each size is its own repository with its weights. Larger sizes give sharper, steadier depth; smaller ones run faster. | Model | Repository | Parameters | Download size | |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:| | S | [apple/DepthPro2-S](https://huggingface.co/apple/DepthPro2-S) | 24M | 97 MB | | B | [apple/DepthPro2-B](https://huggingface.co/apple/DepthPro2-B) | 97M | 386 MB | | L | [apple/DepthPro2-L](https://huggingface.co/apple/DepthPro2-L) | 334M | 1.3 GB | | H+ | [apple/DepthPro2-H](https://huggingface.co/apple/DepthPro2-H) | 872M | 3.5 GB | All sizes share a focal length estimator, [apple/DepthPro2-focal](https://huggingface.co/apple/DepthPro2-focal) (23.5M parameters, 94 MB), which loads with each size and predicts the focal length when it is unknown. ## Quick start ```bash pip install "git+https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-depth-pro-2" ``` ```python from functools import partial import torch from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from safetensors.torch import load_file from depth_pro_2 import DepthPro2, load_rgb, upright from depth_pro_2.model import to_normalized_tensor from depth_pro_2.network.fov import FOVEstimator # apple/DepthPro2-S, -B, -L or -H; bfloat16 is how the models run on a GPU. model = DepthPro2.from_pretrained("apple/DepthPro2-H", precision=torch.bfloat16) # The focal length estimator all sizes share, for photos and videos without a focal length. weights = hf_hub_download("apple/DepthPro2-focal", "model.safetensors") model.fov = FOVEstimator(torch.bfloat16) model.fov.load_state_dict(load_file(weights)) model = model.to("cuda").eval() transform = partial(to_normalized_tensor, device=torch.device("cuda")) ``` ### Image ```python # f_px is the focal length recorded in the photo, or None. image, f_px = load_rgb("photo.jpg") depth = model.infer(transform(image), f_px=f_px)["depth"] # meters, (H, W) ``` ### Video ```python import av # 16 frames at a time: one prediction per frame, in order. video = av.open("video.mp4") frames = (transform(upright(f)) for f in video.decode(video=0)) for prediction in model.infer_video(frames): depth = prediction["depth"] # meters, (H, W) ``` Depth is infinite where the scene is infinitely far, such as the sky. The [code](https://github.com/apple-aiml-research/ml-depth-pro-2) has the command line and a live-feed example. ## Results ### Sharpness and temporal consistency Depth Pro 2 outperforms prior work operating on a single frame or multiple frames on sharpness (Boundary F1 score) and temporal consistency (Jitter). Higher F1 and lower jitter are better, so the top right is best. Results averaged over Sintel and Spring datasets. ### Photos ![Depth Pro 2 on photos: the inputs on top, their predicted depth below](assets/teaser.jpg) Top row: the input photos. --- library_name: liteparse pipeline_tag: image-to-text license: other license_name: ocria-nano-1-license license_link: LICENSE language: - multilingual tags: - ocr - pdf - markdown - document-parsing - tables - layout - onnx - cpu - liteparse - parsebench ---

OCRia-nano-1

Technical report · Blog post · LiteParse · OCRia-1 · ParseBench

OCRia-nano-1 is an 8.1M-parameter model pipeline for document parsing on CPU from [LlamaIndex](https://www.llamaindex.ai). It pairs a detector–recognizer OCR stack with LayoutNet, a joint table and layout model, and it runs inside [LiteParse](https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse), the open-source local document parser. Its models are distilled from [OCRia-1](https://huggingface.co/llamaindex/OCRia-1), our 4B document VLM, with 1/500th of its parameters. - **Accuracy:** 59.2 on [ParseBench-2](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench), ahead of the CPU parsers Indra (55.1) and Marker (52.5). It lifts LiteParse from 48.7 with Tesseract. See [Benchmarks](#benchmarks). - **Speed:** 27.8 pages per second on 16 vCPUs, 426 ms per page on one core, twice as fast as LiteParse with Tesseract. - **Tables and layout:** LayoutNet finds tables (rows, columns, spanning header cells) and classifies layout blocks (headings, lists, captions, page headers and footers) on scanned and born-digital pages. - **Scripts:** a router sends each text line to one of four recognizers: Latin, CJK, right-to-left (Arabic, Hebrew), and a world-script model for about 17 more scripts. - **CPU runtime, everywhere LiteParse runs:** the CLI, Python and Node.js on Linux, macOS and Windows, and the browser and edge runtimes through WebAssembly. > [!NOTE] > These are the model files LiteParse runs; they are not a standalone model with its own inference script. LiteParse > renders the page, runs the detector, router and recognizers, merges the OCR text with the PDF text layer, runs > LayoutNet, and writes Markdown or JSON with bounding boxes. Use them through LiteParse (see [Quickstart](#quickstart)).

## Examples Text lines detected on scanned pages, colored by the recognizer the router picked for each line:

LayoutNet's layout blocks on two multi-column pages, from the PDF text layer alone:

## Quickstart Install LiteParse (`pip install liteparse`, `npm i -g @llamaindex/liteparse` or `cargo install liteparse`), then pull the models once. `lit models pull` downloads this repository's files and ONNX Runtime and checks every file against its pinned sha256; after that, OCRia-nano-1 is LiteParse's OCR backend by default. ```bash lit models pull ocria-nano # once: models + ONNX Runtime (60-75 MB) lit parse scan.pdf --format markdown # OCR, tables and layout with OCRia-nano-1 lit parse scan.pdf --ocr-backend tesseract # force Tesseract for one run ``` ### Python ```python from liteparse import LiteParse, models models.pull("ocria-nano") result = LiteParse(ocr_backend="ocria-nano", output_format="markdown").parse("scan.pdf") print(result.text) ``` ### Node.js ```typescript import { LiteParse, models } from "@llamaindex/liteparse"; models.pull("ocria-nano"); const result = await new LiteParse({ ocrBackend: "ocria-nano", outputFormat: "markdown" }).parse("scan.pdf"); console.log(result.text); ``` ### Browser and edge (WebAssembly) WASM and edge runtimes fully support OCRia-nano. You can also control which models download to minimize download sizes. ```typescript import init, { LiteParse, OcriaNano } from "@llamaindex/liteparse-wasm"; await init(); const ocria = await OcriaNano.fromUrl(); // or { scripts: ["latin"], layout: false } for 1.5 MB of models const parser = LiteParse.withOcriaNano({ ocrEnabled: true, outputFormat: "markdown" }, ocria); const result = await parser.parse(pdfBytes); ``` ### Input - PDFs, images and Office documents (through LiteParse's conversion) - Pages render at 250 DPI for OCR by default (`--dpi` changes it). - Language detection is automatic, the router in OCRia-nano picks a recognizer per line. ### Output LiteParse's Markdown, text or JSON. With OCRia-nano-1: | Content | How it is written | |---|---| | Tables | Markdown tables, or HTML with `colspan` / `rowspan` for spanning cells | | Headings and lists | Markdown headings and list items, from LayoutNet's layout classes | | Page headers and footers | removed from the Markdown by default, kept with `--keep-headers-footers` | | Layout blocks | with `--extract-blocks`, JSON blocks (heading, paragraph, table, figure, ...) with boxes and links to their text items | | Words and lines | JSON text items with bounding boxes and OCR confidence | ## How it works | Model | File | Role | Parameters | |---|---|---|---:| | Line detector | `det.onnx` | segmentation map of text lines, depthwise-separable | 0.08M | | Script router | `router.onnx` | picks a recognizer per line crop, and detects upside-down lines | 0.04M | | Latin recognizer | `rec_latin.onnx` | CTC, int8, supports 791 characters | 0.80M | | World-script recognizer | `rec_world.onnx` | CTC, about 17 scripts | 0.98M | | RTL recognizer | `rec_rtl.onnx` | CTC, Arabic and Hebrew |

--- base_model: Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B library_name: peft license: apache-2.0 datasets: - harness-hub/scale800-harbor - harness-hub/harness-adapters - harness-hub/termgrade-train-harbor - ai-and/termgrade-environments tags: - trl - grpo - async-grpo - lora - agents - harbor - openenv - pi pipeline_tag: image-text-to-text --- ![](banner.png) A LoRA adapter for [Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B), trained with reinforcement learning to work as the model behind the [pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) coding agent on software-engineering and terminal tasks. > [!Tip] > **Most of the gain of maximum-effort thinking, at a quarter of the tokens.** With thinking off, this adapter > matches the base model thinking at its highest reasoning effort (`xhigh`) on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (56.6% vs 54.2%), > and gets 25 of thinking's 35 points on SWE-bench Pro (64.7% vs 74.5%), while generating about 4.5× fewer tokens per > task. See [Thinking vs no thinking](#thinking). - **SWE-bench Pro (hard 51):** 39.2% → 64.7% (+25.5 points; 15 tasks newly solved, 2 lost). - **Terminal-Bench 2.1:** 39.5% → 55.8% (+16.3 points; 16 newly solved, 2 lost). - **Close to thinking-level accuracy, without thinking:** level with the base model at its highest reasoning effort on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 10 points behind on SWE-bench Pro, with about 4.5× fewer generated tokens. - **Less work per task:** under half the turns of the base model on the tasks both solve. > [!Note] > All results are under the pi harness: one attempt per task, a 100-step budget, thinking off unless stated, text only > (the vision tower is not served), sampling at temperature 0.8 with top-p 1.0 (the training sampling). Base model and > adapter always run under identical settings. These numbers are not comparable with the ones on the > [Qwen3.8-27B card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B), which uses other harnesses (Terminus, Claude Code), > thinking at maximum effort, larger budgets and the full SWE-bench Pro. Full recipe will be shared in [the release blogpost](https://huggingface.co/blog/harness-adapters-at-scale) for anyone to build their own harness adapter. **Pick your setup** [![Results](https://img.shields.io/badge/results-pass%401_%2B_efficiency-555?style=flat)](#results) [![transformers](https://img.shields.io/badge/serve-transformers-ffd21e?style=flat)](#use-with-transformers) [![vLLM](https://img.shields.io/badge/serve-vLLM-30A2FF?style=flat)](#use-with-pi) [![llama.cpp](https://img.shields.io/badge/run-llama.cpp-1f1f1f?style=flat)](#use-with-llama-cpp) [![Llama.app](https://img.shields.io/badge/macOS-Llama.app-7f7f7f?style=flat)](#run-with-llama-app) [![GGUF](https://img.shields.io/badge/download-GGUF-ff9d0b?style=flat)](https://huggingface.co/harness-hub/Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted-GGUF) [![Merge](https://img.shields.io/badge/merge-PEFT-ffd21e?style=flat)](#merge) [![Training](https://img.shields.io/badge/training-recipe-4b44c4?style=flat)](#training) [![Trajectories](https://img.shields.io/badge/trajectories-bucket-ff9d0b?style=flat)](#trajectories) A real SWE-bench Pro task under pi: the base model searches and re-runs snippets until it hits the 100-step limit; this adapter finds the function, edits it, runs the tests and fixes the last case, in 8 tool calls. ![](trajectory.gif)
Still version, and the task ![](trajectory.png) Task: `instance_ansible__ansible-d62496fe416623e88b90139dc7917080cb04ce70` from SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), fix `human_to_bytes`. Both runs are from the evaluation above: the base model was graded 0, this adapter 1. Each line is one tool call as the trajectory recorded it, cut to fit.
## Results ![](card-pi.png) | Benchmark | Qwen3.8-27B | Qwen3.8-27B, `xhigh` thinking | **Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted** | Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted, `xhigh` thinking | |---|---|---|---|---| | SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) | 39.2% | 74.5% | **64.7%** | 74.5% | | Terminal-Bench 2.1 | 41.0% | 54.2% | **56.6%** | 56.6% | On Terminal-Bench 2.1 the four runs are compared on the 83 tasks all of them graded, so the base model and adapter scores differ slightly from the paired results below, which use the 86 tasks those two graded. "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default reasoning effort (`xhigh`).
Full paired results (intervals and sign tests against the base model) One attempt per task, thinking off, paired against the base model under pi on the same tasks. The interval is 95%; the p-value is an exact sign test on the tasks that changed outcome. | Benchmark | Tasks | Qwen3.8-27B | Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted (step 160) | Difference (points) | Newly solved / lost | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) | 51 | 39.2% | 64.7% | +25.5 ± 14.2 | 15 / 2 (p = 0.0023) | | Terminal-Bench 2.1 | 86 | 39.5% | 55.8% | +16.3 ± 9.1 | 16 / 2 (p = 0.0013) | | Terminal-Bench 2.1, the 68 tasks not used to pick the checkpoint | 68 | 39.7% | 55.9% | +16.2 ± 10.6 | 13 / 2 (p = 0.0074) | - **SWE-bench Pro (hard 51):** the 51 hardest tasks of [SWE-bench Pro](https://huggingface.co/datasets/harness-hub/swebench-pro-v2-hard51-harbor), 2 h and 100 agent steps per task. - **Terminal-Bench 2.1:** all 89 tasks of [Terminal-Bench 2.1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/harborframework/terminal-bench-2.1), 1 h and 100 agent steps per task. Step 160 was picked by looking at the checkpoints' scores on SWE-bench Pro and on an 18-task subset of Terminal-Bench 2.1, tracked during training.
Work per solved task (turns, visible content, reasoning and generated tokens) Medians per task, this adapter / the base model, over the tasks both solved: same tasks, same outcome, so the numbers measure only how much work each needed. Generated tokens are everything the model writes (visible content, reasoning and tool calls); content is the visible text between tool calls. | | Tas

🤗 Hugging Face   |   🤖 ModelScope

## Introduction We introduce **Ling-3.2-air**, an open-weight model that shares the same native multimodal architecture as [**Ling-3.0-flash-VL**](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.0-flash-VL). Compared with its predecessor, Ling-3.2-air shows stronger performance in workflow automation and reasoning over professional documents. Its **AutomationBench-AA** score rises from 15.7% to **61%**, while its **GDP.pdf** all-pass rate increases from 8.4% to **16%**. On **AA-Briefcase v1.1**, its Elo rating rises from 987 to **1340**, a gain of **353 points**. On **Terminal-Bench 4.0**, its pass rate on terminal-based tasks rises from 0% to **27%**. Overall, **Ling-3.2-air** scores **23** on the **Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1**. Specialized evaluations highlight **Ling-3.2-air**’s performance in quantitative data analysis and legal work. On **Harvey LAB-AA v1.1**, it earns an **87.7%** criterion pass rate. Its all-pass rate is **8.3%** before the material hallucination check and **0.8%** after it. ## Model Overview The model summary information and architecture diagram are as follows:
ArchitectureHybrid-linear MoE
Parameter ScaleTotal 124B, Activated 5.5B
Transformer Layers35 KDA + 7 Gated MLA (5:1)
Number of Dense Layers2
Number of Routed Experts512
Number of Shared Experts1
Number of Activated Experts8
Attention Heads32
Hidden Size2560
Expert Intermediate Size768
Dense Intermediate Size6144
Vocabulary Size157184
## Quickstart ### SGLang (Recommended) The day-0 SGLang image includes Ling-3.2-air support, MTP (NEXTN) speculative decoding, and Hopper decode optimizations: ```bash docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:dev-Ling-3.0-flash-VL ``` #### Run Inference Recommended recipe with 256K context, on 4× 141GB-class GPUs (H20-3e / H200) or 4-GPU Blackwell nodes (B300 / GB300): ```bash docker run --rm --gpus all --ipc=host --shm-size 32g \ -p 30000:30000 \ lmsysorg/sglang:dev-Ling-3.0-flash-VL \ python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path inclusionAI/Ling-3.2-air \ --tp 4 \ --context-length 262144 \ --speculative-algorithm NEXTN \ --trust-remote-code \ --reasoning-parser auto \ --tool-call-parser auto \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 30000 ``` On 80GB cards (H100 / H800), scale out to `--tp 8`. The reasoning and tool-call parsers resolve automatically to `ling3` from the chat template; you can also set them explicitly with `--reasoning-parser ling3 --tool-call-parser ling3`. **Client** It is recommended to use the sampling parameters (`temperature=1.0`, `top_p=0.95`, `top_k=20`) and set `enable_thinking` to `true` for better performance. ```bash curl -s http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "inclusionAI/Ling-3.2-air", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/image.png"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this image in one sentence."} ] }], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": true}, "stream": true, "temperature": 1.0, "top_k": 20, "top_p": 0.95 }' ``` Video input uses `{"type": "video_url", "video_url": {"url": "..."}}` in the same message shape. ### vLLM #### Environment Preparation ```bash pip install uv uv venv ~/my_ling_env source ~/my_ling_env/bin/activate git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/vllm-ling-v3.git cd vllm-ling-v3 VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install --editable . --torch-backend=auto ``` #### Run Inference **Server** ```bash vllm serve "$MODEL_PATH" \ --port "$PORT" \ --trust-remote-code \ --served-model-name auto \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --mamba-cache-mode align \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser ling3 \ --reasoning-parser ling3 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' ``` **Client** It is recommended to use the sampling parameters (`temperature=1.0`, `top_p=0.95`, `top_k=20`) and set `enable_thinking` to `true` for better performance. ```bash curl -s http://${MASTER_IP}:${PORT}/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "auto", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/image.png"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this image in one sentence."} ] }], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": true}, "stream": true, "temperature": 1.0, "top_k": 20, "top_p": 0.95 }'
